title: Investing 101
tagline: Stocks, bonds, funds and compounding how ordinary people build long-term wealth.

instructor.name: Daniel Okafor
instructor.title: CFA charterholder
instructor.bio: Daniel spent 12 years in asset management before switching to investor education. He specialises in explaining markets without the jargon that keeps ordinary people out.

outcomes: Explain what stocks, bonds and funds actually are
Understand the risk–return trade-off and why diversification works
Calculate compound growth and why starting early beats starting big
Tell index funds from ETFs and know why fees matter

lessons.title: Stocks, Bonds and Funds
lessons.content:
## The three ingredients of almost every portfolio

**A stock** is a slice of ownership in a company. When the company profits and grows, your slice becomes more valuable; many companies also share profits directly as **dividends**. Stocks offer the highest long-term growth of the three and the bumpiest ride.

**A bond** is a loan you make to a government or company. They pay you interest on a schedule and return your money at the end. Bonds are steadier than stocks, but steady is not risk-free: prices fall when interest rates rise, and a weak borrower can default.

**A fund** bundles many stocks or bonds into one purchase. Instead of picking winners, you buy the basket instantly diversified, managed either by humans (active funds, higher fees) or by rules that track an index (passive funds, low fees).

### Why this matters

You do not need to predict which company wins. Owning the whole basket through a low-cost fund has, historically, beaten most professional stock-pickers after fees. That is not a hack it is just arithmetic: markets minus low costs beat markets minus high costs.

> **Key idea:** stocks for growth, bonds for stability, funds for diversification. Most long-term investors own all three, blended to match their timeline and stomach for risk.

lessons.title: Risk, Return and Diversification
lessons.content:
## The price of admission

Risk and return are joined at the hip: higher expected return is the **reward for tolerating uncertainty**. Any product promising high returns with no risk is not an investment it is a red flag.

### The two kinds of risk

**Market risk** the whole market falls. Wars, recessions, rate shocks. You cannot diversify this away; you survive it with time horizon and nerves.

**Specific risk** one company or one country collapses. This one you *can* diversify away. Own hundreds of companies across sectors and regions, and no single failure can sink you.

### Diversification, in one sentence

Do not put all your eggs in one basket and do not pay anyone extra to watch the basket.

### Matching risk to your life

- **Money needed in 20+ years** (retirement at 25) can ride out storms: mostly stocks.
- **Money needed in 5 years** (a house deposit) cannot: more bonds and cash.
- **Money needed next month** should not be invested at all that is your emergency fund's job.

> The biggest risk for most beginners is not a crash. It is **panic-selling in one** locking in a temporary fall as a permanent loss. Time in the market beats timing the market.

choices: A loan you make to a government or company that pays interest
questions.explain: Bonds are loans: you lend money, they pay interest on a schedule and return principal at maturity. Steadier than stocks, but not risk-free.

questions.q: What does a fund give you that a single stock does not?
questions.explain: One purchase, hundreds of holdings. No single company's failure can sink a diversified fund.

choices: Specific risk of one company or country collapsing
questions.explain: Specific risk diversifies away. Market risk does not you manage that with time horizon, not stock-picking.

questions.q: Money you need next month should be…
choices: In your emergency fund or cash, not invested
questions.explain: Short-term money cannot ride out a downturn. Investing works on timelines of years, not weeks.

lessons.title: Watch: Compound Interest Explained in One Minute
lessons.content: Sixty seconds that explain the most powerful force in finance. Then read the next lesson to see what it does to real money over real decades.

lessons.title: The Power of Compounding
lessons.content:
## Growth on growth on growth

**Compounding** means your returns start earning returns of their own. In year one, you earn interest on your deposit. In year two, you earn interest on the deposit *plus last year's interest*. The curve bends upward, slowly at first, then dramatically.

### Starting early beats starting big

Two savers, same 7% average return:

- **Amina** invests $200 a month from age 25 to 35 then stops entirely. Total paid in: $24,000.
- **Omar** waits until 35, then invests $200 a month until 65. Total paid in: $72,000.

At 65, Amina who invested a third as much typically ends up **ahead**, because her money compounded for 40 years instead of 30. Time is the ingredient money cannot replace.

### Try it yourself

Open the **compound interest calculator** in Tools. Enter $200 a month at 7% for 30 years, then 40. The difference between the two lines is the entire argument for starting now with whatever you have.

> **Rule of 72:** divide 72 by your annual return to get the years needed to double your money. At 7%, money doubles roughly every 10 years.

lessons.title: Index Funds and ETFs
lessons.content:
## Buying the whole haystack

An **index fund** simply copies a market index like the S&P 500 or a global stock index instead of paying managers to pick winners. An **ETF (exchange-traded fund)** does the same job but trades on an exchange all day like a single stock.

For a beginner, the practical differences are small. The important shared features:

- **Diversification** one fund can hold hundreds or thousands of companies.
- **Low cost** passive funds often charge 0.03–0.2% a year, versus 1%+ for active funds.
- **No crystal ball needed** you own the market's overall return, minus a tiny fee.

### Why fees deserve their own paragraph

Fees compound too against you. A 1% annual fee sounds small, but over 30 years it can consume **a quarter or more** of your potential ending wealth. Costs are one of the few things in investing you can actually control.

### A sensible beginner shape

Many educators point to a simple default: a low-cost global stock index fund for growth, optionally blended with a bond fund as you near your goal. Boring, automatic, diversified and historically very hard for professionals to beat after their fees.

> This is education, not advice: the right mix depends on your country, taxes, timeline and temperament. The principles diversify, keep costs tiny, stay the course travel everywhere.

choices: Returns earning returns of their own over time
questions.explain: Each period's gains are added to the base, so the next period's growth is calculated on a bigger number. The curve bends upward over decades.

questions.q: Using the Rule of 72, how fast does money double at 8% a year?
questions.explain: 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years. A quick mental tool for any growth rate.

questions.q: Why do low fees matter so much over 30 years?
choices: Fees compound against you and can consume a quarter or more of ending wealth
questions.explain: A 1% annual fee drags every year's compounding. Over decades the lost growth dwarfs the fee itself.

questions.q: What does an index fund do?
choices: Picks the ten best stocks each year
Copies a market index at very low cost
questions.explain: Index funds track a whole market passively. You get the market's return minus a tiny fee which beats most active managers after their costs.
